==============================================================================
FILE: mspm0g3507/arduino-core-test/README.md | Community Arduino core for TI MSPM0 on the LP-MSPM0G3507
==============================================================================

# Community Arduino core for TI MSPM0 on the LP-MSPM0G3507

Partly. The core (`tako0910/arduino-mspm0` 0.1.3) installs through Arduino's normal Boards Manager, and a serial sketch and the unmodified Arduino_GFX graphics benchmark ran on the board. But its default build drops the C library's system calls, `analogRead` does not link, and ArduinoJson does not compile, so a beginner hits a wall on three common sketches.

Terms: [vocab](../../docs/vocab.md). Questions and fixes: [FAQ](../FAQ.md). Checked 2026-10-06 on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, arduino-cli 1.5.1 (Homebrew), core `ti:mspm0` 0.1.3 with its own GCC 15.2.1 (arm-none-eabi). Board: LP-MSPM0G3507 with the Waveshare 3.5inch Capacitive Touch LCD wired as in [display-test](../display-test/README.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

## How to install it

The core's Boards Manager URL:

```text
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tako0910/arduino-mspm0/master/package_ti_mspm0_index.json
```

Add it under Arduino IDE Settings, "Additional boards manager URLs", then install "Texas Instruments MSPM0 Arduino Core" in Boards Manager. From a terminal:

```text
arduino-cli core update-index --additional-urls https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tako0910/arduino-mspm0/master/package_ti_mspm0_index.json
```

```text
arduino-cli core install ti:mspm0 --additional-urls https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tako0910/arduino-mspm0/master/package_ti_mspm0_index.json
```

Board name: `ti:mspm0:lp_mspm0g3507` (the LP-MSPM0C1104 is also listed). The core with its compiler took 1.1 GB on disk. Install time was not measured.

## What compiled and what ran

| Sketch | Compiles | Flash, RAM | On the board |
|---|---|---|---|
| `serial_hello` (this repo's) | Yes | 4.8 kB, 112 B | **Runs**: printed a line every second, `millis` steps of about 1,002 ms per line (includes print time) |
| Blink (core example) | Yes | not recorded | Not flashed |
| `light_sensor` (this repo's, `analogRead`) | **No**, link error | | |
| ArduinoJson 7.4.3 JsonParserExample, JsonGeneratorExample | **No** | | |
| OneButton SimpleOneButton | **No** (example has no pin for this board) | | |
| Adafruit FT6206 CapTouchPaint (with Adafruit ILI9341) | Yes | 15.2 kB | Not flashed (ILI9341 screen, not the one used here) |
| Adafruit GFX GFXcanvas | Yes | 16.7 kB | Not flashed |
| Adafruit ILI9341 graphicstest | Yes | 23.1 kB | Not flashed |
| Arduino_GFX PDQgraphicstest, ST7796 pins (this repo's: `sketches/pdqgfx_st7796`) | **Only with LTO off** | 61.3 kB, 784 B | **Runs, unmodified library**: drew on the screen and printed timings |

The benchmark was still running when the 70 s serial capture ended, so these lines finished: screen fill 10.32 s (five fills, so about 2.06 s each), text 0.51 s, pixels 11.7 s, lines 11.4 s. This repo's Arduino layer ran the same benchmark's screen fill in 2.55 s (0.51 s each, see [Arduino layer](../../portability/arduino/README.md)). **Unknown (suspected: Third-party behavior).** The core's SPI clock or transfer loop is likely slower. Not checked: which.

## Problems, with their causes

**The default build fails to link anything that uses stdio.** **Third-party behavior.** The core builds with `-flto`, and link-time optimization discards the core's own `_read`, `_write`, `_close`, `_fstat`, `_isatty` and `_lseek` (in `variants/LP_MSPM0G3507/variant_syscalls.c`). The link then fails with `undefined reference to '_write'` and `dangerous relocation: unsupported relocation`. Fix that worked: build with LTO off by passing the core's own flags without `-flto`:

```text
arduino-cli compile --fqbn ti:mspm0:lp_mspm0g3507 --build-property "build.flags.common=<the core's flags without -flto>" --build-property "build.flags.ld=<the core's link flags without -flto>" <sketch>
```

Copy the two flag lines from the core's `platform.txt` (`build.flags.common` and `build.flags.ld`) and delete `-flto`. Adding system-call stubs of this repo's to the sketch instead failed with `multiple definition of '_read'` once LTO stopped dropping the core's, so do not add stubs.

**`analogRead` does not link.** **Third-party behavior.** The error is `undefined reference to 'DL_ADC12_setClockConfig'` from the core's `MspM0Platform.c`, with or without LTO. The core wraps TI's DriverLib for I2C, SPI, UART, timers and others (`cores/arduino/dl_*_wrap.c`) but has no ADC wrapper, so TI's ADC driver is never built. Not fixed here.

**ArduinoJson does not compile.** **Third-party behavior.** `error: 'Printable' in namespace '::' does not name a type`: the core's Arduino API does not provide the `Printable` class that ArduinoJson expects.

**OneButton's example does not compile.** **Setup or handling.** `error: 'PIN_INPUT' was not declared in this scope`: the example defines its button pin only for boards it lists. Adding `-DPIN_INPUT` through `compiler.cpp.extra_flags` did not reach the sketch with this core. The right property was not found. Editing the example to define `PIN_INPUT 18` (S1, PA18) is the expected user step.

## How this compares with this repo's Arduino layer

The [Arduino layer](../../portability/arduino/README.md) of this repo is built with TI's compiler and ran the same Arduino_GFX benchmark about four times faster on screen fill, but it is a project folder, not something a user installs from Boards Manager. The community core is the real Arduino experience, and with the LTO fix it ran an unmodified popular graphics library on a TI chip.

==============================================================================
FILE: mspm0g3507/display-test/README.md | Waveshare 3.5inch Capacitive Touch LCD on the TI LP-MSPM0G3507
==============================================================================

# Waveshare 3.5inch Capacitive Touch LCD on the TI LP-MSPM0G3507

It works: 12 jumper wires (13 if you read the screen back), a 7.4 kB program, a full-screen redraw in 0.36 s at 8 MHz SPI and 67 ms at 40 MHz SPI (that speed needs an 80 MHz CPU clock set with a SysConfig clock-tree change and 16-bit frames, and only 64 pixels of one row were read back), and touch read from the FT6336U touch chip. Two traps cost most of the time. Chip select needs a pause between commands, because the module's level translator loses short pulses. And the touch chip answered only to software I2C, not the chip's I2C block.

Terms: [vocab](../../docs/vocab.md) and [FAQ](../FAQ.md). The screen's driver chip is the ST7796S, the touch chip is the FT6336U, and the level translator is the TXS0108E, all on the Waveshare module. Checked 2026-10-06 on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, SysConfig 1.26.3, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, OpenOCD xPack 0.12.0. Apple Silicon was not tested. Sizes in kB, 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

Contents: [You need](#what-you-need), [Wiring](#wiring), [Build, flash and read results](#build-flash-and-read-results), [Results](#results), [Performance](#performance-how-fast-it-can-go), [Start-up time](#start-up-time), [Trap 1](#trap-1-the-screen-stays-dark-or-shows-static-even-though-every-wire-is-right), [Trap 2](#trap-2-the-touch-chip-does-not-answer-the-i2c-block-but-does-answer-software-i2c), [Mistakes to avoid](#mistakes-to-avoid).

## What you need

- A TI LP-MSPM0G3507 LaunchPad development kit. The one used here has probe serial `MG350001`; yours will differ.
- The Waveshare 3.5inch Capacitive Touch LCD (320x480) and 13 female-to-female jumper wires.
- MSPM0 SDK, SysConfig and TI Arm Clang installed where `build.sh` expects them (the `SDK`, `CC` and `SYSCFG` lines at its top; change them if yours are elsewhere).
- OpenOCD with a connection file for the board. This repo uses Zephyr's `boards/ti/lp_mspm0g3507/support/openocd.cfg`.
- Python 3 to decode the speed results.

## Wiring

12 wires, no jumpers moved. MISO is an optional 13th wire (J2 pin 14, PB7): wire it only if you want to read the screen's status back, which is how trap 1 was found. Power goes to the 3.3 V pin. Waveshare says supply and signal voltage must match, and this chip's pins are 3.3 V. 5 V was not run.

| Panel pin | LaunchPad header pin (chip pin) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| VCC | 3V3 | 3.3 V supply |
| GND | any GND | |
| SCLK | J1 pin 7 (PB9, SPI1 clock) | Standard-drive pin, so SPI1 here is capped at 16 Mbit/s by the data sheet |
| MOSI | J2 pin 15 (PB8, SPI1 data out) | |
| MISO | J2 pin 14 (PB7, SPI1 data in) | Optional, read-back only |
| LCD_CS | J2 pin 13 (PB6, SPI1 chip select 0) | |
| LCD_DC | J4 pin 39 (PB1) | Plain GPIO |
| LCD_RST | J4 pin 40 (PB4) | Plain GPIO |
| LCD_BL | J4 pin 38 (PA28) | Backlight, GPIO high or PWM |
| TP_SDA | J1 pin 10 (PB3, I2C1 data) | Used as software I2C, see trap 2 |
| TP_SCL | J1 pin 9 (PB2, I2C1 clock) | |
| TP_INT | J2 pin 11 (PB16) | GPIO input |
| TP_RST | J2 pin 12 (PB0) | GPIO output |

Pins to avoid: PA0 (red LED), PB22, PB26 and PB27 (RGB LED), PA18, PB23 and PA9 (buttons), PB24 (thermistor), PA10 and PA11 (backchannel UART). The board's I2C pull-ups for PB2 and PB3 (R59, R60) are not fitted; the software I2C here uses the chip's internal pull-ups. SPI1 and I2C1 use the same pins as TI's own `spi_controller_multibyte_fifo_poll` and `i2c_controller_rw_multibyte_fifo_poll` examples.

## Build, flash and read results

Build every variant into `out/`. Run this in this folder:

```bash
./build.sh
```

It prints, for each build, the address of the `res` results struct (from `tiarmnm`) and the program size. Flash the demo:

```bash
openocd -s <openocd-scripts-folder> -f <openocd.cfg> -c "adapter serial <probe-serial>" -c init -c "reset halt" -c "program out/display_8mhz/display_8mhz.out verify" -c "reset run" -c shutdown
```

Replace `<openocd-scripts-folder>` with OpenOCD's `scripts` folder, `<openocd.cfg>` with the connection file path, and `<probe-serial>` with your kit's probe serial (the text after `usbmodem` in `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*`, minus the last digit). On this bench they were `~/zephyr-toolchain/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7/openocd/scripts`, `~/zephyrproject/zephyr/boards/ti/lp_mspm0g3507/support/openocd.cfg` and `MG350001`. `show.sh` in this folder is a working example for the picture screens.

The demo fills the screen red, green, blue, white and black, draws eight color bars, then paints a white dot wherever you touch and toggles the red LED.

To read the speed results, flash `out/perf/perf.out` the same way, then dump its `res` struct after it has run. The `res` address and size come from `tiarmnm -S out/perf/perf.out` (here: `0x20200280`, 520 B). Reading restarts the program, so do it in one OpenOCD connection with a pause:

```bash
openocd -s <openocd-scripts-folder> -f <openocd.cfg> -c "adapter serial <probe-serial>" -c init -c "reset halt" -c "reset run" -c "sleep 10000" -c halt -c "dump_image mine.bin <res-address> <res-size>" -c shutdown
```

Decode it:

```bash
python3 perf.py mine.bin
```

For the 80 MHz build (`out/perf80/perf80.out`) add the two SPI speeds: `python3 perf.py mine.bin 20,40`. This read command is assembled from the flash command above and the `dump_image` form used elsewhere in this repo; it was not re-run as written.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `display.syscfg`, `gen/` | SysConfig pins: SPI1 3-wire at 8 MHz, I2C1 100 kHz, GPIO for DC, reset, CS, backlight, touch reset and interrupt |
| `display80.syscfg`, `gen80/` | The same at an 80 MHz CPU clock |
| `display_test.c` | The demo, plus the `-DREADBACK`, `-DEXPERIMENT` and `-DDIAG` diagnostics |
| `perf.c`, `perf.py` | Speed test and its decoder |
| `probe.c` | Wire check: each pin read with the chip's pull-up, then pull-down. A loose wire follows the pull |
| `bltest.c`, `bloff.c` | Backlight blink and backlight off |
| `photo.py`, `show.sh` | Turn an image into a screen build and flash a saved one |

## Results

| What | Measured | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Full-screen fill, 300 kB, 8 MHz SPI | 364.9 ms, 84% of the 307 ms the clock allows | perf results struct (32 MHz CPU) |
| Same at 16 MHz | 182.5 ms, 84% of 154 ms | perf results struct (32 MHz CPU) |
| Same at 1 MHz | 2.92 s | observed 2026-10-06; not saved |
| Screen ID read back | `0x7796` (ST7796S), register D3 over MISO | observed 2026-10-06; not saved |
| Touch chip | vendor `0x11` (FocalTech), chip `0x64` (FT6336U), firmware `0x12`, registers A8, A3, A6 | observed 2026-10-06; not saved |
| Touch | dots drawn under the finger, LED toggles per touch | observed 2026-10-06 by the person at the board; not saved |
| Program size | 7.4 kB of flash, 648 B of RAM | `tiarmsize` on the built `display_8mhz.out` |

Colors were not checked by eye at 16 MHz or faster; the panel's data sheet allows about 15 MHz.

## Performance: how fast it can go

Measured 2026-10-06 with `perf.c` in three builds: 32 MHz CPU, 32 MHz CPU with short start-up waits, and 80 MHz CPU. `perf.py` decodes each results struct. Every speed was checked by reading back 64 pixels of one row from the screen's own memory over MISO: 64 of 64 matched at every speed below. That is a spot check, not the whole screen.

| CPU clock | SPI clock | Method | Full screen | Full screens per second | 100x100 box |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 32 MHz | 8 MHz | CPU, 8-bit frames | 364.9 ms | 2.7 | 23.8 ms |
| 32 MHz | 16 MHz | CPU, 8-bit frames | 182.5 ms | 5.5 | 11.9 ms |
| 32 MHz | 16 MHz | CPU or DMA, 16-bit frames | 168.1 ms | 6.0 | 11.0 ms |
| 80 MHz | 20 MHz | CPU or DMA, 16-bit frames | 134.4 ms | 7.4 | 8.8 ms |
| 80 MHz | 40 MHz | CPU or DMA, 16-bit frames | 67.2 ms | 14.9 | 4.4 ms |

- **The wire is the limit.** Every method reaches 84 to 92% of what the SPI clock allows. DMA (a block that copies data without the CPU) is no faster than the CPU loop, but it leaves the CPU free while the screen fills. The free-time measure over-counts, so no percentage is given.
- **40 MHz worked on the standard pins** (with an 80 MHz CPU clock, 16-bit frames and the clock-tree change below). The chip's data sheet promises more than 16 Mbit/s only on its high-speed pins, and the panel's data sheet (ST7796S, 66 ns minimum write cycle) allows about 15 MHz writes. 40 MHz is about 2.7 times that. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Setup or handling).** Only 64 pixels of one row were read back at 40 MHz. Not checked: every pixel, the screen by eye at 40 MHz, longer wires and a second module. So the margin may not hold elsewhere.
- **16-bit frames need the SPI block switched off to change.** Setting the frame size while SPI is enabled did nothing, silently. **Tag: Tool or docs.** The `DL_SPI_setDataSize` documentation does not say so.
- **80 MHz needs the clock tree, not the default line.** `display80.syscfg` is a copy of TI's `sysctl_mclk_syspll` clock tree. With `SYSCTL.forceDefaultClkConfig` left in, SysConfig ignored every clock setting and stayed at 32 MHz. **Tag: Tool or docs.** SysConfig gave no warning.

### Start-up time

| | Power-up to screen ready | To first full frame |
|---|--:|--:|
| Usual init (120 ms waits after reset, software reset and sleep out) | 370 ms | 538 ms at 16 MHz; 461 ms seen once, not saved |
| Shortest waits the ST7796S data sheet allows (`-DFAST_BOOT`) | 12 ms | 180 ms at 16 MHz, 79 ms at 40 MHz SPI with the 80 MHz CPU clock |

The chip itself starts in 0.26 to 0.31 ms (data sheet SLASEX6C, cold start-up). Almost all of the usual 370 ms is waits copied from common drivers. The screen's power-mode register read `0x9C` (awake, display on) after the fast init too.

### Running code from external memory

Not possible on this chip. **Tag: Chip limit.** The MSPM0G3507 data sheet lists no external memory bus or quad-SPI interface, so code must fit in its 128 kB of flash. External SPI flash or the display's SD slot can hold pictures, fonts and logs, streamed in over SPI. The LP-MSPM0G3519 has 512 kB of flash and 128 kB of RAM.

### LVGL on this screen

Yes, trimmed. LVGL (an open-source graphics library) runs on this chip with this screen: 25.1 kB of RAM, 125.4 kB of flash at 32 MHz (126 kB at 80 MHz), and 7 refreshes per second at 32 MHz and 15 to 19 at 80 MHz. A refresh redraws only the changed areas (about 12,000 to 25,000 pixels), so it is not a full-screen update; the full-screen figures above are for filling all 153,600 pixels. Details: [lvgl-g3507](../lvgl-g3507/README.md).

## Trap 1: the screen stays dark or shows static, even though every wire is right

Measured: each command sent alone took effect; sent back to back, the second was lost. The code raised chip select for a few hundred nanoseconds between two commands, and "display on" was always the second one, so the screen never turned on. Status reads over MISO showed it. A 10 µs pause after chip select goes high fixed it (`cs_gap()` in `display_test.c`). Slowing the SPI clock does not help, because the pulse is between bytes, not in them.

**Tag: Unknown (suspected: Third-party behavior).** The module puts a TXS0108E level translator between the header and the screen, and the suspect is that it does not pass a pulse that short, so the screen saw two commands as one. Not checked: the pulse on a scope, and a module without the translator.

## Trap 2: the touch chip does not answer the I2C block, but does answer software I2C

**Tag: Unknown (suspected: Third-party behavior).** With the chip's I2C1 block, every read of address 0x38 failed: first not acknowledged, later the controller reported the bus busy. The same two pins driven as plain open-drain GPIO, bit by bit at about 100 kHz, got an acknowledgement and correct registers every time, so the demo uses software I2C. The suspect is the same level translator on an open-drain bus.

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Tag: Third-party behavior.** Calling `DL_GPIO_initPeripheralInputFunctionFeatures` to add a pull-up rewrites the whole pin register and clears the open-drain setting that SysConfig's code sets next with `DL_GPIO_enableHiZ`. Call `DL_GPIO_enableHiZ` again after it. Fixing that alone did not make the I2C block work here.
- Switch an output pin off before reading it back in a wire check, or a good wire looks wrong (`probe.c` does).

How the faults were found without a scope: the probe showed every display wire connected and the unwired control pin floating; the backlight test gave a yes or no a person can see; and wiring MISO let the chip read the screen's ID and power-mode register after every step (`-DEXPERIMENT`), which isolated the dropped commands in one run.

==============================================================================
FILE: mspm0g3507/lvgl-g3507/README.md | LVGL on the TI LP-MSPM0G3507 with 32 kB of RAM
==============================================================================

# LVGL on the TI LP-MSPM0G3507 with 32 kB of RAM

**Status: Works (serial numbers).** Built and run on the board 2026-10-06. The screen picture and touch were not checked by eye in this run, so only the serial numbers are claimed.

Yes, trimmed. LVGL 9.6 with a button, slider, switch, arc, chart and one font runs on the LP-MSPM0G3507 using 25.1 kB of its 32 kB of RAM and 125.4 kB (32 MHz build) or 126 kB (80 MHz build) of its 128 kB of flash. It refreshes 7 times a second at 32 MHz with the CPU about 100% busy, and 15 to 19 times a second at 80 MHz with 40 MHz SPI and the CPU about 60% busy. A refresh redraws only the parts of the screen that changed, not the whole screen. RAM is not the problem; flash is. The second font and a few LVGL drawing paths had to be cut to fit.

Terms: [vocab](../../docs/vocab.md) and [FAQ](../FAQ.md). LVGL is an open-source C graphics library for small screens. A refresh is one pass in which LVGL redraws only the areas that changed and sends them to the screen; in these logs that is about 12,000 to 25,000 pixels, against 153,600 pixels in the full 320 x 480 screen. The heap is the pool LVGL takes its memory from. The draw buffer holds the strip of pixels being drawn. The stack is the RAM for function calls. Built and run 2026-10-06 on an Intel Mac with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 and SysConfig 1.26.3. Sizes are bytes unless marked kB; 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. The screen is the Waveshare 3.5inch Capacitive Touch LCD wired as in [display-test](../display-test/README.md) (the pin table is there).

Contents: [Results](#results-on-the-board), [Build and flash](#build-and-flash), [On the LP-MSPM0G3519](#on-the-lp-mspm0g3519), [Sizes](#sizes), [Choices](#the-choices-and-why), [What did not fit](#what-did-not-fit-and-what-was-cut), [What was not checked](#what-was-not-checked).

## Results on the board

Each build was read for 19 complete stats lines over about 21 seconds. The first 32 MHz line has three stray characters in front, and the last 80 MHz line is cut where the capture stopped. Defaults: 12 kB heap, 6 kB stack, 6.2 kB draw buffer. Flash and RAM are the `tiarmsize` totals of the 2026-10-06 builds.

| Build | Refreshes per second | CPU busy | Refresh (one pass) | Flush (SPI send) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 32 MHz CPU, 16 MHz SPI | 7 | 96 to 105% | 137 to 150 ms | 27.5 to 27.8 ms |
| 80 MHz CPU, 40 MHz SPI | 15 to 19 | 58 to 62% | 32 to 39 ms | 5.6 to 7.1 ms |

- **Heap:** peak 8.5 kB used at both 32 and 80 MHz, in a pool LVGL reports as 10.3 kB usable (a 12 kB pool). That leaves about 1.8 kB of headroom over the peak in these runs.
- **Stack:** `port.c` paints the stack with `0xA5A5A5A5` at boot. After the demo had run about 20 seconds, 2.1 kB of 6 kB were untouched on both builds, so the peak was 3.9 kB. The peak covers the idle demo's redraws; nobody used the touch screen, so the button, slider and full-redraw paths are not covered.
- **RAM total** with 6 kB stack and 12 kB heap: 25.1 of 32 kB.
- **What a refresh covers:** the `px` field is pixels sent to the screen per second: 172,086 to 174,381 at 32 MHz (about 24,600 to 24,900 per refresh) and 233,674 to 237,037 at 80 MHz (about 12,400 to 15,600 per refresh). A full screen is 153,600 pixels, so one refresh is a fraction of the screen. Refreshes per second are not full-screen frames per second; [display-test](../display-test/README.md) measured full-screen fills at 6.0 and 14.9 a second.
- **Busy above 100%:** `busy` is exactly refreshes per second times the average refresh time, divided by a fixed 1,000 ms (`app.c`). In all 38 lines `fps` times `refr_ms` divided by 10 matches `busy` within 1 point (for example 7 x 145.0 ms = 1,015 ms, shown as 101%). Seven refreshes of 145 ms cannot fit in 1,000 ms, so the real window was a little longer than one second. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Our mistake).** The one-second stats window probably runs late: the stats timer runs after a 145 ms refresh, and the `t=` counter skips a second twice in the 32 MHz file (no `t=5s`, `t=22s`) and once in the 80 MHz file (no `t=6s`), which fits a window longer than 1 s. The window length was not logged. Read the 32 MHz result as "the CPU is saturated", not as a number above 100%.
- **Serial line length:** a stats line is about 180 characters, so by arithmetic about 15 ms to send at 115,200 baud, and sending blocks the main loop.

Each 80 MHz refresh also sends only 50 to 63% of the pixels of a 32 MHz refresh, so refresh and flush times are not like for like. Per pixel, flush is about 2.5 times faster (about 1.1 µs at 32 MHz, about 0.45 µs at 80 MHz), which matches the change from 16 MHz to 40 MHz SPI. The CPU clock was not read back.

## Build and flash

What is here: `lv_conf.h` (the trimmed LVGL settings), `src/port.c` (1 ms tick, ST7796S flush over SPI1 with DMA, FT6336U touch over software I2C, UART text, stack paint), `src/app.c` (the demo), `syscfg/` (SysConfig for 32 MHz and 80 MHz, same pins as `display-test` plus UART0), `build.sh`, `tools/mapsize.py` (flash and RAM split from the map) and `tools/host_check.sh` (renders the screen on the Mac). LVGL v9.6.0, commit `80ca777e37a2b176770726a02e07a6fb79ef0b39`, MIT license (`third-party/lvgl/LICENCE.txt`), is vendored once for every board in `third-party/lvgl/` with unused parts removed. Three small size patches (12 added lines in three files) are in `size-patch.diff`. `host-render.png` is the screen as rendered on the Mac by the same `app.c`; it is not a photo of the board.

Build the three flashable variants. Run this in this folder:

```bash
./build.sh
```

| Build | CPU | SPI clock | `.out` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lvgl_32mhz` | 32 MHz | 16 MHz | `out/lvgl_32mhz/lvgl_32mhz.out` |
| `lvgl_80mhz_spi40` | 80 MHz | 40 MHz | `out/lvgl_80mhz_spi40/lvgl_80mhz_spi40.out` |
| `lvgl_80mhz_spi20` | 80 MHz | 20 MHz | `out/lvgl_80mhz_spi20/lvgl_80mhz_spi20.out` |

Options go before the command, for example `OPT=-Os`, `ROWS=20` (draw buffer rows), `MEM_KB=12` (LVGL heap in kB), `STACK=6144` (bytes). The defaults are 12 kB heap and 6 kB of stack. LVGL compiles once per variant (about a minute), then each config links in seconds. `./build.sh oversize` builds the full-feature demo only to measure it; it does not fit and must not be flashed.

The 40 MHz SPI clock is about 2.7 times the panel's write spec of about 15 MHz (ST7796S data sheet, 66 ns minimum write cycle). **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Setup or handling).** [display-test](../display-test/README.md) read back 64 pixels of one row correctly at 40 MHz, and the LVGL runs above sent data at that speed, but nobody looked at the screen. If it shows noise at 40 MHz, try `lvgl_80mhz_spi20`, which was built but not run.

Flash one build. The values in angle brackets are this bench's examples, and you substitute yours. `<out>` is one of the `.out` paths above. `<openocd-scripts-folder>` was `~/zephyr-toolchain/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7/openocd/scripts`, `<openocd.cfg>` was `~/zephyrproject/zephyr/boards/ti/lp_mspm0g3507/support/openocd.cfg`, and `<probe-serial>` was `MG350001`; yours is the text after `usbmodem` in `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*`, minus the last digit.

```bash
openocd -s <openocd-scripts-folder> -c "gdb_port disabled" -c "tcl_port disabled" -c "telnet_port disabled" -f <openocd.cfg> -c "adapter serial <probe-serial>" -c init -c "reset halt" -c "program <out>" -c "reset run" -c shutdown
```

This programs without `verify`: on these images OpenOCD's verify reported a CRC mismatch ([FAQ](../FAQ.md)), and the programmed images ran.

Read the serial output (UART0 through the probe, 115200 8N1) with any terminal program. The board's serial port is the `/dev/cu.usbmodem` device whose name ends in 1; the one ending in 4 is not used. For example:

```text
screen /dev/cu.usbmodem<probe-serial>1 115200
```

You get a boot banner `LVGL on LP-MSPM0G3507: starting`, then one line a second. A real line from the 32 MHz run:

```text
t=4s fps=7 busy=101% refr_ms=145.0 flush_ms=27.8 px=174381 full_ms=0.0 heap_used=7236 heap_total=10536 heap_peak=8712 heap_free=3300 frag=4% stack_free=2200 touch_err=0 presses=0
```

## What the screen is meant to show

Portrait, dark theme, as in `host-render.png` (the Mac render; the board's screen was not checked by eye): a title, a **Press me** button with a counter, a slider that sets the red LED's brightness in 10 steps, a switch that turns the LED on and off, a **Full redraw** button that times one 320 x 480 redraw, an arc and a line chart fed by a made-up wave every 100 ms, and five stats lines refreshed once a second. The `full_ms` value stays `0.0` until someone presses **Full redraw**, so it was not measured.

## On the LP-MSPM0G3519

The same demo runs on the LP-MSPM0G3519 LaunchPad development kit (512 kB flash, 128 kB RAM, same Cortex-M0+ core), with the display wired like this: SPI1 on PB31, PB8 and PB7, chip select PB12, data/command PB9, backlight PC4, reset PC5, touch I2C2 on PC3 and PC2, touch interrupt PB14, touch reset PB11. Build it with:

```text
BOARD=mspm0g3519 ./build.sh
```

Only the board-specific parts are new, in `boards/mspm0g3519/`: `board_pins.h` (reset, backlight and touch pins that moved to port C) and `lvgl.syscfg` and `lvgl80.syscfg` (the display pins plus UART0 on PA10 and PA11, the same backchannel pins as the G3507). `src/`, `lv_conf.h` and the LVGL copy are shared. Output goes to `out/mspm0g3519/`. Checked 2026-10-09, same tools as above.

Results, 3 runs each, 19 to 24 stats lines per run, read from UART0 through the probe at 115200. The 80 MHz build with 40 MHz SPI was seen on the screen; the other builds' screens were not looked at. Rows are in `data/results/mspm0g3519.csv`.

| Build | Refreshes per second | CPU busy | Refresh | Flush | G3507 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 32 MHz CPU, 16 MHz SPI | 7 | 96 to 105% | 138 to 151 ms | 27.5 to 27.8 ms | 7 |
| 80 MHz CPU, 40 MHz SPI | 15 to 19 (mean 17.1) | 57 to 61% | 32 to 39 ms | 5.6 to 7.1 ms | 15 to 19 |
| 80 MHz CPU, 20 MHz SPI (1 run) | 13 to 18 (mean 15.6) | 63 to 71% | 36 to 52 ms | 10.6 to 16 ms | not run |

The runs of one build were identical line for line after the boot banner, so the demo is repeatable here. Flash is 125.5 kB at 32 MHz and 126.2 kB at 80 MHz, of 512 kB; RAM is 25.1 kB and 25.2 kB, of 128 kB. Heap peak is 8.5 kB and 2.1 kB of the 6 kB stack stayed untouched, as on the G3507.

With the extra room (1 run each, `ROWS=40 BOARD=mspm0g3519 ./build.sh`): a 40-row draw buffer (25 kB) raises the 32 MHz build from 7 to 11.8 refreshes a second on average (10 to 13), because LVGL sends fewer, larger strips; at 80 MHz it stays at 15 to 19 and the CPU drops to 43% busy, so something other than drawing sets the rate there. The cause was not found. The full demo with the second font (`BOARD=mspm0g3519 ./build.sh oversize`, 146.8 kB of flash) also runs at 7 a second at 32 MHz. It is the stock demo with this repo's size cuts left in, not an unmodified LVGL.

Two gotchas. The G3519's linker script sets a 256-byte stack, so `build.sh` now rewrites whatever stack size the script holds; the first build kept 256 bytes and its log showed `stack_free=0`. And the G3519 build prints `LVGL on LP-MSPM0G3519: starting` as its banner; a serial capture keeps everything the previous firmware printed before the reset, so cut the log at the banner.

## Sizes

| | 32 MHz build | 80 MHz, SPI 40 | 80 MHz, SPI 20 | Oversize (not flashable) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Flash used | 128,456 (125.4 kB) | 129,072 (126.0 kB) | 129,072 (126.0 kB) | 150,264 (146.7 kB) |
| Flash free of 131,072 | 2,616 (2.6 kB) | 2,000 (2.0 kB) | 2,000 (2.0 kB) | -19,192 (-18.7 kB) |
| RAM used (`.bss` + `.data` + stack) | 25,733 (25.1 kB) | 25,733 | 25,733 | 25,733 |
| RAM free of 32,768 | 7,035 (6.9 kB) | 7,035 | 7,035 | 7,035 |

All four are `tiarmsize` totals from builds made 2026-10-06 after the stats buffer grew from 160 to 256 bytes (96 bytes more RAM than the first builds, which were 25,637). Flash split for the 32 MHz build, from the map file (`tools/mapsize.py`):

| Part | Flash | RAM |
|---|--:|--:|
| LVGL | 122,052 (119.2 kB), of which fonts 13,649 | 12,288 (the 12 kB heap, `LV_MEM_SIZE`) |
| Port (`port.c`) | 1,744 | 6,417 (draw buffer 6,400, counters 17) |
| App (`app.c`, `main.c`) | 2,107 | 348 (the 256-byte stats buffer is most of it) |
| SysConfig and startup | 768 | 0 |
| C library | 1,785 (what remains of the total) | 536 (rest of `.bss`) |
| Stack (linker) | 0 | 6,144 |
| Total | 128,456 | 25,733 |

The 80 MHz builds are 616 bytes bigger in flash. The map shows 300 of them in the SysConfig and startup code, which holds the clock setup; the other 316 were not traced.

## The choices, and why

- **Heap 12 kB, draw buffer 320 x 10 rows (6.2 kB), stack 6 kB.** One partial buffer in RGB565, no double buffering. Ten rows is the size that was built and run; more rows mean fewer strips per redraw but more RAM. `ROWS=20` was not built; by arithmetic it adds 6.2 kB of RAM and leaves 635 bytes (0.6 kB) free. The heap peak is measured (8.5 kB); the stack peak is measured (3.9 kB).
- **No byte swap.** The SPI block sends one 16-bit frame high byte first, which is the order the ST7796S wants, so LVGL's native RGB565 goes straight to DMA, as in `display-test/perf.c`.
- **DMA with a blocking wait.** One buffer means the CPU cannot render the next strip while DMA sends this one. DMA is no faster than a CPU loop here (the wire is the limit, see display-test), so it is used to free the CPU bus, not for speed.
- **16-bit frames need the SPI block off to change size.** `frames16()` disables SPI, sets the size, and enables it again around every strip. **Tag: Tool or docs.** The `DL_SPI_setDataSize` documentation does not say so.
- **Chip select gap of 10 µs after every raise.** **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Third-party behavior).** The suspect is the module's level translator dropping shorter pulses ([display-test trap 1](../display-test/README.md#trap-1-the-screen-stays-dark-or-shows-static-even-though-every-wire-is-right)).
- **Touch by software I2C at about 100 kHz,** polled every 20 ms, because the I2C block never got an answer ([display-test trap 2](../display-test/README.md#trap-2-the-touch-chip-does-not-answer-the-i2c-block-but-does-answer-software-i2c)). **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Third-party behavior).** A read that is not acknowledged keeps the last touch state and counts as a touch error.
- **1 ms SysTick** feeds `lv_tick_set_cb`. The same interrupt runs a 10-step software PWM on the red LED (PA0, assumed active high, as in TI's `gpio_toggle_output`). The main loop is `lv_timer_handler()` then `__WFI()`.
- **`-Oz`.** `-Os` was 8,544 bytes (8.3 kB) bigger than `-Oz` before the size patch, so only `-Oz` is known to fit. `-Oz` is slower than `-O2`; no speed was measured.
- **LVGL config** (`lv_conf.h`): software renderer only, RGB565 only, no ARGB8888 or A8 destinations, no float, no OS, no log, no file system, no image decoders, no flex or grid, no sysmon, default theme (dark) only, 14 px Montserrat.

## What did not fit, and what was cut

**Tag: Unknown (suspected: Chip limit).** The 128 kB flash is where the full demo stops. LVGL is made of many small pieces, so no one function is large and there is no single thing to remove. The build got under the limit by removing a font and drawing features. So this says what fits in this build, not the most any build could fit.

The builds, in the order they were made (flash in bytes, chart and arc in every one):

| Build | Flash |
|---|--:|
| `-O2`, Montserrat 14 and 24, ARGB8888 and A8 drawing on, stock LVGL | 266,768 (260.5 kB) |
| `-Os`, Montserrat 14 and 20, ARGB8888, A8 and other formats off in `lv_conf.h` | 178,976 (174.8 kB) |
| `-Oz`, same | 170,432 (166.4 kB) |
| `-Oz`, size patch (no shadow, blur, layer, triangle, mask-rectangle or image drawing, no image decoder), Montserrat 20 dropped | 133,504 (130.4 kB) |
| Same, plus no image-format glyphs in `lv_draw_sw_letter.c` | 128,464 (125.5 kB) when measured; 128,456 in the final build (8 bytes less, from later small changes that were not isolated) |

Montserrat 20 costs 21,808 bytes (21.3 kB): the oversize build below, 146.7 kB, is the final demo with that font added back. The size patch is worth 20,168 bytes (19.7 kB) with that font in both builds (166.4 kB down to 146.7 kB). The oversize build is 19,192 bytes (18.7 kB) over the chip's flash; it links only into a pretend 512 kB flash for measuring and must not be flashed.

The patch assumes the demo draws no images, shadows or layers. A widget that needs one draws nothing for that part, and the image decoder is not initialized, so code that opens an image would misbehave. None of this demo's widgets do; the Mac render shows the screen drawing correctly. Rounded corners, the arc and the chart all stayed in. Other font sizes were not run.

`-flto` was accepted and the output was byte for byte identical. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Tool or docs).** TI Arm Clang may ignore `-flto` for this link. Its documentation was not checked.

## What was not checked

- The screen by eye: display init, colors, orientation. Only serial numbers were read.
- Touch through LVGL: the saved runs show `touch_err=0` and `presses=0` on all 38 lines, which means the touch chip answered every read, but nobody touched the screen. Coordinates, orientation and what a finger does to the button and slider were not run by a person.
- LED polarity (PA0 assumed active high) and the slider's effect on brightness.
- DMA through LVGL's buffer: the flush time was measured, but the pixels were not compared.
- The `lvgl_80mhz_spi20` build: built, not run.
- Software I2C timing at 80 MHz: its delay scales with the CPU clock, so it should still be about 100 kHz; not measured.
- `-Os` after the size patch: only `-Oz` was built with it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Tag: Our mistake.** Do not start with a 2 kB stack. Use 6 kB. A 2 kB stack ran out (`stack_free=0`, no untouched bytes), and a 4 kB stack left 152 bytes at the measured peak of 3.9 kB, so 2 kB was overrun by about 1.9 kB.
- **Tag: Our mistake.** Do not size the heap from a 64-bit Mac run. The measured peak on the chip is 8.5 kB, so 12 kB is enough here.
- **Tag: Our mistake.** Keep the serial stats buffer at 256 bytes. The stats line is 176 to 179 characters, so a 160-byte buffer cuts every line in the demo's own code (`static char line[256]` in `src/app.c`). The serial link is not the cause.

==============================================================================
FILE: mspm0g3507/zephyr/README.md | Zephyr blinky on the LP-MSPM0G3507 from an Intel Mac
==============================================================================

# Zephyr blinky on the LP-MSPM0G3507 from an Intel Mac

Zephyr 4.4.2 `samples/basic/blinky` ran on the LP-MSPM0G3507 and the blue LED blinked. Checked 2026-10-05. The first run took about 9.5 minutes of machine time from nothing installed, with no hands-on time. A script now does the same install in about 3 minutes.

Terms: [vocab](../../docs/vocab.md) and [FAQ](../FAQ.md). Sizes in kB, 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

![Build memory report and the start of the flash](../screenshots/z5-zephyr-build-memory-report-and-flash.png)

Build size from the memory report: 11.7 kB of flash, 3.9 kB of RAM. `west flash` found the probe, detected the chip and wrote 11.7 kB. The LED pin read back as toggling three times, a second apart.

## Official steps that did not work here

Four places where the official instructions failed on this Intel Mac. Each one is a step a newcomer would have to work out alone.

| # | The official way | What blocked it | What was done instead |
|---|------------------|-----------------|-----------------------|
| 1 | Install build tools with Homebrew | Homebrew builds from source on this Intel Mac | `pip install west cmake` in a Python 3.12 environment. `dtc` left out; the build does not need it. |
| 2 | `west sdk install` for the compiler | Zephyr SDK 1.0.1 has no Intel macOS build, and Zephyr 4.4.2 requires SDK 1.0. The command fails with an empty list. | Arm compiler from SDK 0.17.4 via `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=cross-compile`, plus the `picolibc` module. Works. Not an officially supported pairing. |
| 3 | Clone OpenOCD and build it from source | Needs a build toolchain this Mac does not have | Prebuilt xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7, which already supports the chip and the XDS110 probe. |
| 4 | `west flash`, then watch it blink | After a debugger soft reset the chip sat in Zephyr's NMI handler, no blink | One board-level reset command. The reset button does the same. |

Two safety checks to make before flashing a borrowed board, neither in any guide: confirm the fix for the December 2025 "bricked LaunchPad" bug (Zephyr PR 102668) is in the source, and confirm the image contains main flash addresses only.

Done differently by choice, to save time and disk: a pinned release (v4.4.2), shallow clones, and only four modules instead of a full `west update`.

## Repeat it

`./setup.sh` is the cross-platform version: macOS on Intel or Apple silicon and Linux on x86_64 or arm64, every download pinned and checksummed, Python 3.12 from uv when the machine has none, a free-disk check first. From nothing installed, build only: 2 min 48 s on this Intel MacBook inside a sandbox that hides every installed tool, 56 s on an M4 Mac, 93 s in an Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 container on that Mac (all 2026-10-18). Linux x86_64 is pinned but not run. The flash leg on Apple silicon and on Linux is untested.

`./setup-intel-mac.sh` is the exact sequence that worked on the Intel Mac, with checksums. It ran from clean twice on 2026-10-05, in a plain Terminal window: 3 minutes 00 seconds and 3 minutes 06 seconds, exit code 0 both times. The first run, while the workarounds were still being found, took 9.5 minutes.

![Script finished in 3 minutes 6 seconds](../screenshots/z8-zephyr-script-finished-3m06s.png)

## Red blink

`red-blink/` is a copy of the blinky sample that lives in this repo instead of the Zephyr tree. Two changes: `boards/lp_mspm0g3507.overlay` points `led0` at the red channel of the RGB LED (PB26) instead of blue (PB22), and `SLEEP_TIME_MS` is 500, so the LED is on half a second and off half a second.

Build and flash, with the environment from `setup-intel-mac.sh`:

```text
cd ~/zephyrproject/zephyr
west build -p always -b lp_mspm0g3507 <this repo>/zephyr/red-blink -d ../build-red-blink
west flash -d ../build-red-blink --openocd "$OCD/bin/openocd" --openocd-search "$OCD/openocd/scripts"
```

Then do the board-level reset from step 6 of the script. It took 85 seconds to build and 7 to flash and reset. CCStudio can stay open with no debug connection; it does not get in the way.
